# Memory, Perception & Attention

<!-- Generated by packages/rules/generate.mjs from data/laws/*.json. Do not edit by hand. -->

11 card(s). Check the code in front of you against each one that applies.

## MPA-01 — Serial Position Effect

- **Axiom:** Humans recall items positioned at the beginning and end of sequences most reliably.
- **Apply when:** Critical navigation or actions sit mid-list and are overlooked while first and last items dominate attention.
- **Check:**
  - Put critical destinations at the far left or top and far right or bottom of navigation.
  - Place core value propositions in the first rows and conversion actions in the last.
  - Pin frequent dropdown options to the top and summary categories to the bottom.
- **Instead of:** A 12-item flat navigation menu buries the primary analytics dashboard in the middle.
- **Do:** Group the 12 items into five to seven top-level destinations (DEC-01), then put Dashboard first and Settings last.
- **Source:** Bennet B. Murdock Jr. (1962), *The Serial Position Effect of Free Recall*.

## MPA-02 — Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect)

- **Axiom:** An item that differs from its neighbors is remembered better than the items around it.
- **Apply when:** One row, button, or price is remembered while identical neighbors blur together.
- **Check:**
  - Emphasize one item per view; every extra highlight competes with the one meant to stand out.
  - Match the emphasis to the decision: the row people must recall gets the weight.
  - Test recall a day later, when the standout item is what remains. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** Every plan card is bright blue, so none of the three is remembered.
- **Do:** Only the recommended plan is filled; the other two stay outlined.
- **Source:** Hedwig von Restorff (1933), *Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld*.

## MPA-03 — Zeigarnik Effect

- **Axiom:** Unfinished tasks stay in memory longer than tasks already completed.
- **Apply when:** People return days later and remember exactly where they stopped.
- **Check:**
  - Save progress automatically and offer to resume where the person stopped.
  - Show unfinished items on return; do not make people hunt for them.
  - End a session with a visible next step, not a blank confirmation.
- **Instead of:** A half-finished application vanishes on reload, so the person starts over.
- **Do:** The draft is saved and the return screen names the next question.
- **Source:** Bluma Zeigarnik (1927), *Über das Behalten von erledigten und unerledigten Handlungen*.

## MPA-04 — Peak-End Rule

- **Axiom:** An experience is remembered by its peak and its ending, not its average.
- **Apply when:** A smooth session is rated harshly because its last screen failed.
- **Check:**
  - End every flow on a clear confirmation that names what happens next.
  - Soften the most intense step: the peak sets the rating more than the middle.
  - Fix mid-flow defects on their own terms: a strong ending recolors the memory, it does not repair the experience.
- **Instead of:** A fast checkout ends on a paywall error, so the whole flow is remembered as bad.
- **Do:** The last screen thanks the person and confirms the order.
- **Source:** Daniel Kahneman, Barbara L. Fredrickson, Charles A. Schreiber & Donald A. Redelmeier (1993), *When More Pain Is Preferred to Less: Adding a Better End*.

## MPA-05 — Anchoring Bias

- **Axiom:** An initial number pulls later estimates toward it, even when it is arbitrary.
- **Apply when:** A suggested price, quantity, or budget shifts what people choose.
- **Check:**
  - Remove arbitrary defaults before asking for an estimate.
  - Show a reference range the evidence supports, not a number near the answer.
  - Test the same question with and without a starting figure. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** A donation field prefilled with the highest tier lifts every gift.
- **Do:** The field starts empty and offers a range with its basis.
- **Source:** Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman (1974), *Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases*.

## MPA-06 — Selective Attention and Attentional Bottleneck

- **Axiom:** Attention admits one channel at a time; unattended channels survive only as fragments.
- **Apply when:** Two simultaneous requests compete, and the second is missed entirely.
- **Check:**
  - Route interruptions to one channel instead of stacking toasts and modals.
  - Do not put two demands in the same moment; queue the second.
  - Keep a missed request recoverable where the person will look for it.
- **Instead of:** A toast, a modal, and a banner ask for attention at once.
- **Do:** One request at a time, queued in a place the person can revisit.
- **Source:** Donald E. Broadbent (1958), *Perception and Communication*.

## MPA-07 — Confirmation Bias

- **Axiom:** People seek and weight evidence that confirms what they already believe.
- **Apply when:** A dashboard shows only the runs that support the current plan.
- **Check:**
  - Show disconfirming results at the same prominence as confirming ones.
  - Ask what evidence would change the decision before the test runs. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
  - Record every run, including the ones that refute the hypothesis. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** Only successful test runs are shown, so a failing design looks proven.
- **Do:** Report all runs, with refutations beside the successes.
- **Source:** Raymond S. Nickerson (1998), *Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises*.

## MPA-08 — Sunk Cost Fallacy

- **Axiom:** Money already spent pulls the next decision, though only future costs should.
- **Apply when:** A team keeps funding a feature because of what it has already cost.
- **Check:**
  - Name the cost already spent and leave it out of the go/no-go calculation.
  - Judge the next step by what it costs from here and what it returns.
  - Rewrite a stuck decision as if nothing had been spent yet, then compare.
- **Instead of:** A failing feature keeps its budget because half of it is already built.
- **Do:** Decide on the remaining cost and return; note the spent money and exclude it.
- **Source:** Hal R. Arkes & Catherine Blumer (1985), *The psychology of sunk cost*.

## MPA-09 — Loss Aversion

- **Axiom:** Losses weigh on choices more than equivalent gains do.
- **Apply when:** A change is refused for what it might lose, not weighed by what it gains.
- **Check:**
  - Show the loss and the gain of a change side by side, in the same units.
  - Describe what staying costs as plainly as what moving costs.
  - Test whether the framing moved the decision, not only the preference. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** A migration is presented only as what could break, so nobody approves it.
- **Do:** State the risk and the gain together, with the same visibility and the same units.
- **Source:** Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky (1979), *Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk*.

## MPA-10 — Goal-Gradient Effect

- **Axiom:** Effort rises as the goal nears; the last stretch gets the most.
- **Apply when:** People start slowly on a long task and speed up near its end.
- **Check:**
  - Show how far the person has come, not only how much remains.
  - Split a long run into visible goals, so a near one is always in reach.
  - Put the last review beside the finish, where the end is in view.
- **Instead of:** A ten-step setup shows one spinner for the whole run, so people leave at step three.
- **Do:** Show each completed step and the count remaining, so the goal stays in view.
- **Source:** Ran Kivetz, Oleg Urminsky & Yuhuang Zheng (2006), *The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention*.

## MPA-11 — Status Quo Bias

- **Axiom:** People keep the option they already have unless something forces a change.
- **Apply when:** A setting nobody changed is treated as the one people chose.
- **Check:**
  - Name the default in words and say what happens if nobody chooses.
  - Make any move away from the default reversible in one step.
  - Give the alternatives the same visibility as the default; do not bury them.
- **Instead of:** Opt-out sits on a second screen, so the default is the only path anyone finds.
- **Do:** Show the default and the alternative on one screen, equally visible, both one click away.
- **Source:** William Samuelson & Richard Zeckhauser (1988), *Status quo bias in decision making*.
